analysis.one_liner: Extends and expands federal compensation for people sickened by nuclear weapons testing fallout, uranium mining, and Manhattan Project waste.
analysis.headline: The bill to compensate nuclear-test downwinders and uranium workers has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since January 2025 with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The Radiation Exposure Compensation Act pays people who got cancer after being exposed to radiation from nuclear weapons testing or uranium mining. This bill would restart and enlarge that program: it raises payments to $100,000, covers more people (including uranium workers through 1990, residents of areas near Manhattan Project waste in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky, and Guam downwinders), adds more covered cancers and kidney diseases, gives claimants five years instead of two to file, and funds research into uranium mining's health effects. It was introduced with support from senators of both parties but has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: People who developed cancers or kidney disease after living downwind of nuclear tests, working in uranium mines and mills (including core drillers and workers with combined work histories), or living near Manhattan Project waste in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky — plus their surviving spouses and children, who can claim after a death. Previously compensated people could collect the difference under the higher award.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwinders, uranium miners, and their families

how_it_helps.text: New compensation for people who lived in designated ZIP codes near Manhattan Project waste sites in Missouri, Tennessee, Alaska, and Kentucky who later developed specified cancers: $50,000 or more for living victims, plus reimbursement of documented out-of-pocket medical costs, and $25,000 to the spouse or children of someone who died.
Raises the standard award for leukemia and other specified cancers linked to nuclear testing from $50,000-$75,000 to a flat $100,000, and lets previously paid claimants collect the difference.

Expands uranium-worker eligibility: covers workers employed through 1990 instead of 1971, adds core drillers and remediation workers, recognizes combined work histories across mining jobs, and adds kidney diseases to the covered conditions.

Gives claimants five years instead of two to file, lets denied claimants resubmit, accepts affidavits as evidence of work history and presence in affected areas, and requires the Justice Department to accept tribal records like grazing permits and homesite leases as proof of residency.
Adds chronic lymphocytic leukemia as a covered disease and extends eligibility to Guam and new downwind areas.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through the compensation fund's extension and the higher $100,000 award, plus appropriations for research grants and studies. The government pays because it conducted the tests and supported the mining.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the per-claim award to $100,000 and extends the fund six years, adding significant federal spending at a time of large deficits; the Justice Department administers claims, and expanded categories like combined work histories and renal disease will increase both payments and administrative burden.

Establishing that a cancer was caused by nuclear testing or uranium work decades ago is inherently uncertain; the bill relaxes evidentiary standards, for example by allowing sworn affidavits to supplement employment and residency records and by extending eligibility windows to 1990 for uranium work, which broadens compensation beyond cases with strong causal documentation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is real: expanded eligibility and higher payments will cost taxpayers billions over the fund's life, and paying for cancers that are hard to attribute to specific exposure means some payments go to people whose illness may not stem from radiation. But the program exists precisely because the government knowingly exposed workers and communities to radiation while withholding information about the dangers, and full information about those exposures was never made available to the people affected. Against that history, the cost is a deliberate policy choice to make whole a group of citizens the government's own activities harmed, rather than a loophole.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has remained with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: The only action on the bill since introduction is that it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on January 24, 2025.
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote have occurred in the 119th Congress so far.

The underlying Radiation Exposure Compensation Act had lapsed claim-filing windows and limited coverage, which this bill would fix by extending the fund six years, extending the claim-filing period to five years, and adding new affected areas and diseases.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet and no one has definitively lost; the people whose cancer claims would be compensated are left waiting, and the only party spared cost so far is the Treasury, since the fund has not been extended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; claims remain unpaid

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend RECA claims and add compensation for Missouri residents near Manhattan Project waste.

for.name: Sens. Luján, Heinrich, Kelly, Crapo, and Schmitt
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill support from both parties.

for.name: 6 of 45 Senate Democrats and 2 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship and cosponsorship run across party lines, from Republican senators from Missouri and Idaho to Democratic senators from New Mexico and Arizona, reflecting the geography of nuclear testing and uranium work rather than party ideology.

industries.note: The bill does not regulate the industry; it makes the federal government, rather than the companies, pay the lifetime medical and cancer costs that uranium work produced, effectively absorbing an old industry's liability as a public obligation.
The expanded compensation, fund extension, grants, and studies are all funded by appropriations, so the public treasury bears the cost of compensating for harm done in the government's name.

analysis.trajectory: With a bipartisan group of sponsors and an identical bill that cleared the Senate in the previous Congress, the bill has a plausible path if the Judiciary Committee or Senate leadership schedules action; but with no committee activity more than a year into the Congress, the more likely outcome is that it stalls again unless attached to a larger must-pass bill.
